sources.title: RIT CSCI-632 Mobile Robot Programming catalog description
sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.content: This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Course offered every other year. Prerequisites: CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

sources.title: ROS 2 Concepts
sources.author: Open Robotics
sources.content: ROS 2 organizes a robot application as nodes that communicate through typed interfaces. Topics support publish-subscribe streams, services support request-response interactions, and actions support longer-running goals with feedback and cancellation. Parameters configure node behavior. Coordinate transforms describe relationships among reference frames. Sensors produce observations that must be timestamped and interpreted in the correct frame. Robot software separates sensing, state estimation, planning, control, and actuation while making message contracts and timing assumptions explicit. Testing should consider latency, dropped messages, sensor noise, actuator limits, safety boundaries, and the difference between simulation and physical operation.

sources.title: OpenCV Documentation
sources.author: OpenCV
sources.content: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, thresholds, coordinate frames, and evaluation metrics.
